co_schoolyard_the_2.blurb: The Schoolyard is a small sport wall inside the Lime Creek limestone canyon, high in the hills south of Eagle and Basalt at roughly 9,200 feet. Its 14 bolted lines cover a friendly spread: a handful of easy to moderate routes in the 5.5 to 5.8 range, then a solid block of 5.10s and 5.11s, topping out with a couple of 5.12s. That mix makes it a handy warm-up or a first stop for newer leaders. It is one of the first walls you meet on the north side of the creek, close to the roadside camp spots, and a short climber's trail through aspens leads to the base.

co_society_turn.blurb: Society Turn is a compact sandstone bouldering cliff a few miles from the town of Telluride, at about 9,000 feet. Of its 14 problems, most are boulders spanning a wide range, from V0 and V1 up through the V7 to V8 zone, with a couple of very hard lines near the top end, plus two harder topped-out lines that are often toproped. The wall sits in the sun and faces south, so it dries out quickly and stays pleasant on bright winter days. It is an easy, quick-access spot for an after-work session, though the area is modest in size rather than a destination.

co_spillway_camp_2_the.blurb: The Spillway and Camp 2 hold 14 granite boulder problems in Elevenmile Canyon, southwest of Colorado Springs and Denver. The problems are scattered around the campsites and on the slope behind them, so a day here is a casual wander rather than a circuit. Grades stay friendly, from VB up to about V4, with most lines in the V1 to V3 range, which suits beginners and warm-up sessions. Landings are mostly flat and soft, and the standout is a V4 starting seated inside a small cave-like tunnel at Camp 2. Bring a pad. The canyon runs colder than most of the Front Range, which keeps summer climbing comfortable.

co_huhly_muhly_boulders.blurb: Huhly Muhly is a small cluster of gneiss boulders in Alderfer/Three Sisters Park, a Jefferson County open space west of Denver near Evergreen. Of its 13 problems, nearly all fall between V3 and V7, so it leans toward intermediate and strong boulderers rather than beginners; the problems are described as fun, with a couple of traverses and a dyno in the mix. The boulders sit on both sides of the Mountain Muhly Trail, a short walk past a few other bouldering spots. The park's western boulders tend to catch direct sun, while the eastern ones lie in shady pine forest.

co_bunker_the.blurb: The Bunker is a steep sport crag on the north side of Clear Creek Canyon, west of Golden, at about 7,500 feet. Its centerpiece is a shaded, north-facing overhanging cave, with the main cave staying out of the sun until late afternoon in summer. The 13 routes here are hard: a couple of 5.11s and one 5.12 as a lead-in, then mostly 5.13 and low 5.14 pumpy, powerful lines with kneebars and heel hooks. A steady breeze keeps it workable through summer. The walk up from the road is steep and tiring, so expect a real hike, and it is a place for strong, experienced sport climbers.

co_left_book.blurb: Left Book is a low-angle slab on the Book, one of the big formations of Lumpy Ridge just north of Estes Park. It holds 13 trad routes, with a good number of moderate lines around 5.7 and a scatter of climbs from 5.5 up to 5.10 and one harder line, which makes it a favorite when you want something more gentle than the steep cracks nearby. Features are subtle, so route-finding takes care. A major ledge system splits the face and serves as the way down. The walk in is long and the final stretch is a steep gully scramble; weekends can bring a crowd.

co_winchester_cave_the.blurb: The Winchester Cave is a small, steep cave in Rifle Mountain Park, the limestone canyon north of the town of Rifle, at about 7,000 feet. All 13 routes are bolted sport lines and every one is hard: a half dozen in the 5.12 range, four around 5.13 and a few in the 5.14 range. Several are well-known testpieces, and a clean vertical wall on the left side of the cave adds variety. The approach is short from the parking area, crossing the stream and then following the base downstream over talus. This is a spot for strong sport climbers rather than anyone working up through the grades.

co_chain_station.blurb: Chain Station is the first ice area to come into shape on the east side of Wolf Creek Pass, sitting just above a large roadside pullout in the San Luis Valley side of the pass at roughly 8,800 feet. It offers 13 climbs split between water ice and mixed, with ice from WI3 to WI5 and mixed lines from M4 to M5. A handful of lines form reliably each winter, and many more are fickle. The wall faces south, so it can get wet and sun-baked, and conditions swing with the weather. Because the base is right by the road, the approach is minimal.
